Our Methodology

A Disciplined Approach to Dispute Resolution

Navigating the Nepalese judicial hierarchy requires methodical preparation and adherence to strict statutory timelines.

⚖

Evidentiary Case Merit Assessment

Prior to initiating legal action, our counsel conduct an exhaustive documentary review under the Evidence Act 2031, calculating statutory limitation periods (Hadmyad) to prevent avoidable dismissals.

📜

Procedural Rigor under Civil & Criminal Codes

Whether formulating a Plaint (Firdi-patra), Written Defence (Pratiuttar-patra), or Bail Application, every pleading is drafted strictly in compliance with Court Rules and judicial precedent.

🛡

Ethical Advocacy & Client Confidentiality

Client communications are protected by rigorous professional privilege in accordance with the Nepal Bar Council Code of Conduct 2051 and the Individual Privacy Act 2075.

Client Journey

The Case Enquiry & Engagement Process

Four transparent steps from initial enquiry to active court representation.

1

Preliminary Enquiry Submission

Submit an overview of your legal query through our secure consultation portal or contact our registry directly by telephone. Please do not submit sensitive evidentiary secrets at this stage.

2

Conflict Check & Advocate Assignment

Our chambers registrar performs an ethical conflict-of-interest check to confirm we do not represent an adverse party, then assigns the matter to specialized legal counsel.

3

Strategic Legal Consultation

Attend a scheduled in-person consultation at our Kathmandu or Itahari chambers (or secure virtual session). We evaluate documents, clarify applicable statutes, and explain procedural options.

4

Formal Vakalatnama & Retainer Agreement

If both parties agree to proceed, formal representation commences upon executing a Vakalatnama (Power of Representation) and a transparent engagement agreement.

Professional Standards & Client Feedback Notice

Common Inquiries

Frequently Asked Legal Questions

Clear answers regarding consultations, fee factors, and court representation in Nepal.

How do I schedule an initial legal consultation in Nepal?

You can schedule an initial consultation by calling our office (+977-1-4240000), using the confidential consultation request form on our website, or emailing consult@pathivaralawfirmitahari.com. We offer in-person consultations at our Kathmandu and Itahari offices, as well as secure virtual consultations via Google Meet or Zoom for clients outside these cities or residing abroad.

Does submitting an enquiry or reading this website establish an advocate-client relationship?

No. Under Nepal Bar Council professional ethics rules, accessing this website, reading our educational resources, or transmitting an electronic enquiry does not create an advocate-client relationship. A formal relationship is created only after an initial conflict check is completed and a formal vakalatnama (power of attorney/engagement agreement) is executed.

What documents should I bring to my first legal consultation?

You should bring government-issued photo identification (Citizenship Certificate or Passport), all original or clear photocopies of relevant contracts, notices, court orders, property documents (such as Lalpurja or blue prints), police reports, and a concise chronological summary of the facts and key dates involved in your matter.

What are the typical stages of a civil lawsuit in Nepal District Courts?

A civil lawsuit under the Muluki Civil Procedure Code 2074 generally follows six stages: 1) Filing of the Plaint (Firdi-patra); 2) Service of Notice / Summons (Myad Jari) to the opposing party; 3) Filing of Written Statement of Defence (Pratiuttar-patra); 4) Evidence Submission & Witness Examination (Praman Parikshan); 5) Final Legal Arguments (Bahas); and 6) Judgment (Faisala) and Decree Execution (Faisala Karyanvayan).

Can criminal charges or police complaints be settled out of court in Nepal?

In Nepal, criminal offenses are strictly divided into State-prosecuted offenses (Government of Nepal is the plaintiff under Schedule 1 of the National Criminal Procedure Code 2074) and Individual-party offenses (Schedule 2/3). State offenses such as fraud, forgery, homicide, and narcotics cannot be legally settled privately. Minor individual offenses or civil-nature disputes may be eligible for statutory reconciliation (Milapatra) where specifically authorized by law.
